transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, my wife actually suggested I come talk to someone. She thinks I'm reading too much into things lately. I know she says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but... well, for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It's like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

It reminds me a bit of how my students communicate, actually—I'm a teaching assistant over at the university, mostly handling the intro sociology seminars. You wouldn't believe how these kids write their essays now. They use these bizarre formatting tricks to try and get past the page count requirements. I spend half my Sunday just fixing their margins and fonts before I can even grade the actual content. And the grading software the department makes us use is constantly crashing anyway. They promised us an update in the spring, but you know how university administration is, everything moves at an absolute snail's pace. So I'm just sitting there hitting refresh on my laptop for twenty minutes... 

Wait, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Right, why I'm here today. Yeah, so, the messages she's sending just... I just know they mean something else.
Have you had any recent head injury, new medical illness, or started any new medications or substances around the time these beliefs began?

No, nothing like that. No head injuries, and I haven't been sick at all. I haven't started any new medications either. I mean, I take an ibuprofen sometimes for my back, but that's just because the chairs in the sociology department are absolutely ancient. They have these awful wooden slats that dig right into your lumbar spine if you sit for more than an hour. 

I actually put in a request with the university facilities office to get one of those ergonomic chairs back in October. But they told me I had to get a formal medical note from a doctor first just to prove I needed it. Can you believe the bureaucracy? A doctor's note just to get a chair that doesn't actively ruin your posture. Meanwhile, my buddy over in the economics department, he got a motorized standing desk his very first week with absolutely no questions asked. They just wheeled it right into his office. It really makes you wonder how they allocate the budget between the different departments, you know? The disparity is just ridiculous, especially when you look at the endowment... 

Wait, sorry. I'm rambling. What were we talking about? Oh, right, medical stuff. But yeah, no, I'm perfectly healthy. No new drugs or illnesses or anything like that.
Have you had a period lasting at least a week where you felt unusually elevated, energetic, or needed much less sleep than usual?

No, not really. I mean, my energy is pretty average. I definitely need my sleep, though getting it is another story lately because the apartment above us just got a new dog. A beagle, I think? It howls at the absolute worst times. I actually ended up reading this whole article the other night about how beagles were specifically bred for hunting, so their vocal cords are adapted to carry over long distances through dense forests. 

The researcher who wrote it was from Cornell, I think, and he went into all this detail about canine genetics. It's really fascinating how much we've manipulated animal DNA just for our own convenience over the centuries. We talk a lot about social constructs in my intro sociology seminars, but the biological constructs are just as wild when you think about it. I was actually thinking of incorporating it into my next discussion group, but the professor I TA for is incredibly strict about sticking to the syllabus. He's one of those old-school guys who still uses overhead projector transparencies. Can you believe that? In this day and age. I have to go down to the university library's basement just to print them for him because the main copiers don't take the plastic sheets... 

Wait, I'm sorry, I lost the thread again. You were asking about my energy? Yeah, no, no weird energy spikes or anything like that. Just my normal self.
Have you ever heard a voice that other people around you could not hear?

No, I've never heard anything like that. No voices or anything. It's just the messages my wife sends, like I said. The text itself is what I'm looking at. I actually spend a lot of time looking at text, honestly. Between her messages and the essays I have to grade, my eyes are constantly strained. 

I actually went to the optometrist last month because I thought I might need bifocals. Getting older, you know? The doctor there was this really intense guy who kept talking about the blue light from screens. He tried to sell me these special glasses with yellow tint on the lenses for like, two hundred dollars. Two hundred! I told him that seemed a bit steep, especially on a TA's stipend. The stipends haven't been adjusted for inflation since 2018, which is just criminal when you look at how much rent has gone up around the campus. The graduate student union has been trying to negotiate a new contract for months, but the administration just keeps stalling. They hire these expensive outside lawyers to come in and sit at the bargaining table, just to tell us there's no money in the budget. But then they turn around and build a brand new athletic center with a smoothie bar...

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? Tangents. What was the question? Voices? Right. No, no voices. Just me in my own head.
Do you think there’s any chance that your wife’s messages might just be normal and you could be misinterpreting them?

No, I don't think I'm misinterpreting them. I know my wife says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but for the past year they've lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It's like there's a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won't say directly. 

Speaking of her office, they actually just renovated the whole floor she works on. They went with this open-concept floor plan, which she hates because there's absolutely no privacy. I read a study recently about open-concept offices, actually. It was in an organizational sociology journal. The study found that instead of increasing collaboration, open offices actually decrease face-to-face interactions by something like 70 percent because everyone just puts on noise-canceling headphones and emails the person sitting right next to them. It completely defeats the purpose. And the noise level! My wife says there's this one guy in accounting who eats crunchy granola bars at his desk every afternoon at 2:00 PM, and it echoes across the whole floor. She actually started bringing earplugs to work just to focus on her reports. 

Which reminds me, I really need to buy more earplugs because of that beagle upstairs. I swear, the walls in our building are made of paper. The landlord promised to put in extra insulation when we renewed our lease, but of course, that never happened. Landlords, right? They'll promise you the moon just to keep you paying rent... 

Sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the messages. But yeah, no, I'm not misinterpreting them. There's definitely a pattern there, a signal she's sending me. It's too precise to just be normal office stuff.
Have you noticed other people saying your speech has become hard to follow or more disorganized lately?

No, I don't think anyone has said that. I mean, my students seem to follow me just fine in my discussion sections. Though, honestly, half the time I wonder if they're even listening to me anyway. If anyone's communication is disorganized lately, it's theirs. 

I was grading these short response papers on Weber's theory of bureaucracy yesterday, and I swear, the grammar is just atrocious. They write their academic essays like they're sending a text message. I actually read this really long piece in the Chronicle of Higher Education last month about how the pandemic completely stunted reading comprehension and writing stamina for this generation. It's genuinely sad. And the university just expects us to pass them anyway because retention rates are directly tied to our state funding. It's all about the metrics now. The dean sent out this massive email last week about "optimizing student success pathways," which is just administrative corporate-speak for "don't fail anyone." 

I tried to bring it up at the department meeting, but the chair just completely brushed past it so they could talk about the upcoming faculty retreat. They're going to this fancy lodge up in the mountains, which is honestly a slap in the face because the TA travel budget got slashed to absolute zero this year. If I want to present my research at the regional conference, I have to pay for the gas and hotel out of my own pocket. And gas prices are just... 

Wait, I'm doing it again. Tangents. I apologize. You asked if people find my speech hard to follow? No, nobody has mentioned anything like that to me. I think I communicate pretty clearly.
Over the past year, have you noticed your work, social life, or self-care getting noticeably worse?

Worse? No, not really. I haven't had any major problems at work, and my self-care is exactly the same as always. I keep my usual routines. I'm up at 6:30 every morning, make my coffee, grade for an hour before I head to campus. I actually just switched to a French press because I read this article about how the paper filters trap all the natural oils from the beans. It really does make a huge difference in the flavor profile, though cleaning the wet grounds out of the glass beaker is a bit of a hassle. You're definitely not supposed to wash them down the sink because it ruins the plumbing. Our building's pipes are from the 1970s, and the super told me last month that if one more person clogs the main line, he's going to start fining the tenants. Which I'm almost positive is illegal under the city's renter protection ordinance. I actually downloaded a PDF of the municipal housing code just to check, because landlords will try to get away with anything if you don't know your rights... 

Wait, sorry. I'm drifting again. The question. Work and self-care. Yeah, they're completely fine. 

The only thing is... well, it has mostly affected my marriage. We've been having these repeated, really tense conversations at home about the messages she's getting. It got to the point where we started seeing a couples therapist. And she—the therapist, I mean—eventually suggested I get an individual assessment. So that's why I'm sitting here. But yeah, outside of the tension with my wife, everything else in my life is running normally.
Have you had any beliefs like this about other people or situations, or is it only about your wife?

No, it's really just about her. I don't have any, you know, suspicions or whatever about my colleagues or my students. Like I said, the students are their own whole issue, but that's just normal academic frustration. It's only my wife and those messages. 

Though, you know, speaking of other people, my brother did try to tell me I was being paranoid a few months ago. He lives out in Denver, and we usually do a Zoom call every other Sunday. He actually just bought this massive, overpriced mid-century modern house out there. The real estate market in Colorado is completely out of control right now. I was looking at Zillow the other day just out of curiosity, and the property taxes alone are more than my entire annual stipend. It's absurd. He works in tech, of course, doing something with cloud architecture, which I still don't fully understand even though he's explained it to me three times. He keeps trying to convince me to leave academia and learn how to code, like it's just that easy. Like you can just drop twenty years of sociological research to go write Python for some startup that's going to go bankrupt in two years anyway. The tech bubble is going to burst again, I keep telling him that. It's basic historical cyclicality, you see it in every major industry boom...

Sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? The tangents. But to answer your question, no. It's just my wife. I don't think anyone else is sending me hidden signals or anything like that. Just her.
During the time this belief about your wife has been present, have you ever had episodes of confusion or feeling like your mind was clouded?

Clouded? No, not at all. My mind feels perfectly clear. I mean, I have to be sharp for my research. Actually, I did start taking this lion's mane mushroom extract a few months ago, just to make sure I stay focused while I'm trying to finish my dissertation. I heard about it on this podcast I listen to on the train. The host was interviewing this neurobiologist from Stanford—or maybe it was Berkeley, I can't remember—but they were talking about neuroplasticity and how these functional mushrooms can stimulate nerve growth factor. It's fascinating stuff, really. 

Though you have to be incredibly careful with the supplement industry because it's completely unregulated by the FDA. You could be buying something that says it's pure extract, and it turns out to be mostly just brown rice flour and mycelium filler. I actually spent about three hours researching third-party lab testing protocols before I finally bought a bottle. They charge an arm and a leg for the good stuff, too. It's like forty dollars for a tiny tincture, which is just absurd on a TA's salary, but you can't really put a price on cognitive longevity, right? Especially with all the microplastics we're ingesting these days. I read an article last week that said they actually found microplastics in the clouds recently. In the actual rain. It just makes you wonder what we're breathing in every single day when we walk outside...

Wait, sorry. I'm rambling again. I do apologize. You were asking if my mind felt clouded or confused? No. I haven't experienced anything like that. I feel completely lucid.
Have you ever felt that anyone other than your wife was trying to send you hidden messages or signals?

No, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anyone else doing anything like that. It's really just the situation with my wife. 

Although, speaking of signals, I did have a very strange interaction with the barista at the coffee shop near campus yesterday. Not a hidden message or anything, just... odd customer service. I ordered an Americano, black, which is what I always get when I don't have time to use the French press I was telling you about. And he handed it to me and said, "Enjoy the ride." Who says that about coffee? "Enjoy the ride." It felt very performative, you know? Like he was trying out a catchphrase. 

It reminds me of this paper I read in grad school about the commodification of emotional labor in the service industry. How we expect retail workers to not just perform a task, but to curate an entire emotional experience for the consumer. It's exhausting for them, obviously. I actually had a student write a brilliant term paper on it last semester, comparing Starbucks baristas to Disney World cast members. She got an A, which I rarely give out because grade inflation is completely destroying the credibility of higher education. If everyone gets an A, then the degree means nothing. I was telling the department chair that at the faculty mixer last month, and he just completely brushed me off. He's retiring next year anyway, so he doesn't care. He's moving to Florida. Naples, I think. Which is just going to be underwater in twenty years anyway with the sea level rising...

Oh, I'm sorry. I did it again. I completely lost the thread. You were asking if anyone else was sending me messages? No. Just her. Nobody else.
When you’re convinced your wife is sending hidden signals, do you also ever feel unusually special or like those messages are meant specifically for you in a grand, important way?

No, not in a grand way. I mean, they're meant for me, obviously, because they're on her social media and we're married, but I don't feel like I'm, you know, the chosen one or something. It's just a personal issue between a husband and wife. 

It's not like that guy I saw on the news last week. Did you see that? The one who climbed the radio tower downtown because he thought the local news anchor was broadcasting a marriage proposal to him through the weather report. They had to get the fire department out there with the ladder truck. The whole thing tied up traffic on I-95 for like four hours. Which is already a nightmare on a good day. I had to sit in gridlock for forty-five minutes just to go three exits when I was driving to the archives last Tuesday. The infrastructure in this city is just crumbling. The potholes on Main Street are getting so bad I think I knocked my car's alignment out of whack. I drive a 2012 Civic, and it's been incredibly reliable, but you hit one of those craters and it just destroys the suspension. I should probably take it in to the mechanic, but you know how they are. You go in for an oil change and suddenly they're telling you that you need new brake pads and a timing belt and it's going to cost eight hundred dollars. It's a complete racket. My dad used to do all his own car repairs, but cars were simpler back then. Now everything is computerized. You need a specialized diagnostic tool just to figure out why the check engine light is on...

Sorry, I'm doing it again. The tangents. But no, I don't feel special or grand about the messages. It's just her trying to communicate with me in this incredibly frustrating, passive-aggressive way.
Have you become noticeably more withdrawn from friends, family, or activities you used to enjoy?

Withdrawn? No, I wouldn't say that. I still show up for all my teaching sections, and I'm keeping up with my data analysis for the department. I still ride my bike everywhere, too. 

Actually, speaking of the bike, the city just put in those new protected bike lanes over on 4th Street, which in theory is a great idea, but they used those cheap plastic bollards to separate the lane from traffic. Delivery trucks just run right over them. Half of them are completely flattened already. It's actually more dangerous now because drivers get confused by the green paint on the asphalt. I was reading an urban planning journal the other day about how shared spaces—where you remove all the signs and lanes completely—actually reduce accidents because everyone is forced to pay attention to each other. It's like that town in the Netherlands where they took out all the traffic lights and accident rates just plummeted. Human psychology is funny like that. People rely way too much on external rules and painted lines instead of just paying attention to what's actually happening right in front of them. 

It's kind of like this guy Martin I play chess with. I still meet up with my friends for chess on Thursday nights, and Martin always uses the exact same Sicilian Defense opening. Every single time. If you just memorize the standard book responses, you can trap his queen by move fifteen. But he refuses to adapt. People just get so incredibly stuck in their routines, you know? They just do the same thing over and over and expect a different result. 

But anyway, sorry, I'm drifting again. To answer your question, no, I haven't withdrawn from my life at all. I'm doing all my normal activities, seeing my friends, doing my research. The main place this whole thing causes trouble is just when my wife and I get stuck arguing about what her work schedule really means. That's where the friction is. Everything else in my life is completely fine.
Have you ever had other unusual experiences, like seeing things other people couldn’t see?

Seeing things? No, definitely not. I mean, my vision is completely fine, no hallucinations or anything like that. I don't see things that aren't there. 

Though, speaking of seeing things, have you noticed those new LED streetlights they just installed all around the campus perimeter? The glare on them is absolutely blinding. It’s this harsh, blue-white light, like a hospital corridor. It completely washes out the night sky. You used to be able to see Orion from the quad on a clear winter night, but now it's just this dome of artificial light pollution. And it’s actually terrible for the local ecosystem. I was reading in one of the environmental science journals—I sometimes help proctor their large lecture midterms—about how that specific wavelength of light completely disrupts the circadian rhythms of nocturnal insects. Which then, of course, cascades right up the food chain to the bats. 

We actually have a pretty significant bat population living in the belfry of the old humanities building. They had to delay the entire roof renovation last summer because it turned out to be a protected maternity roost. The contractors were absolutely furious. They were losing thousands of dollars every week the scaffolding just sat there unused, but federal wildlife laws are pretty strict about that sort of thing. You can't just evict an endangered species because you want to put down some new asphalt shingles. It became this whole political thing with the university administration and the biology department...

Oh, wow, I am so sorry. I completely derailed again. My brain just jumps from one thing to the next. But to answer your question, no, I've never seen anything that other people couldn't see. Just the regular world.
Has this belief about your wife caused you to miss work, stop seeing friends, or otherwise change how you live your life?

Miss work? No, not at all. I haven't missed a single day. I'm keeping up with everything—work, self-care, my usual routines. I mean, my morning routine is pretty dialed in. I make my pour-over coffee at exactly 6:30 every morning. I use this manual burr grinder I found at a thrift store—it's a vintage German model, solid metal construction. You just can't buy things made like that anymore. Everything now is cheap plastic with planned obsolescence built right in. 

Like our toaster. I bought a new toaster two years ago and the heating element on the left side is already completely dead. It just burns one side of the bread and leaves the other side raw. It's absurd. We generate so much e-waste as a society. I read an article last month about how these massive shipping containers full of broken appliances just get dumped in landfills overseas, and the heavy metals leach right into their groundwater. It's a total environmental catastrophe that nobody wants to take responsibility for, all because companies want us buying a new twenty-dollar toaster every other year... 

Sorry. I'm doing it again. The toaster. Anyway, no, my routines are totally fine. The only real change, or the main place it's causing problems, is just at home. It's mostly affected my marriage. We just keep having these incredibly tense conversations about it. It actually got to the point where our couples therapist eventually suggested I get an individual assessment. So that's why I'm here, really. But as far as my job or my friends or taking care of myself? No, all of that is perfectly fine.
Do you ever believe that someone outside your marriage is controlling your thoughts, actions, or feelings?

Controlling my thoughts? No, definitely not. My thoughts are completely my own. Nobody is literally putting thoughts in my head or making me do things. 

Though, I suppose if you want to get philosophical about it, the algorithms on the internet are basically trying to do that to everyone these days, right? You search for one thing—like, the other day I was looking up replacement parts for that vintage burr grinder I mentioned, specifically a ceramic burr set, because the steel ones can actually heat up the beans if you grind too fast and it completely ruins the extraction profile of a light roast. Anyway, I search for that one time, and suddenly every single website I visit is pushing artisanal coffee paraphernalia at me. It's wild how predictive analytics work. The big tech companies have essentially mapped human impulse control. I was actually reading a paper published by a colleague in the sociology department about how these recommendation engines don't just predict behavior, they actively shape it by creating these tight little feedback loops where people only see things that reinforce their existing biases... 

But, ah, sorry. There I go again. I know what you were actually asking. To answer your question literally, no, no one is controlling my feelings or my actions. I'm completely in control of my own mind.
Have you ever felt like your thoughts were being taken over or put into your mind by an outside force?

Taken over? No, I think that's pretty much the same as what you just asked, right? My thoughts are entirely my own. Nobody is inserting things into my brain. 

Although, I will say, when I'm grading undergraduate essays, I sometimes wonder if their thoughts are being put into their minds by an outside force. Specifically, AI. I was grading this massive stack of midterms for the Intro to Poli Sci course I TA for, just last weekend actually, and I swear, a dozen different students used the exact same robotic phrasing about the rapidly evolving geopolitical landscape. It drives me absolutely crazy. You can spot the generated text a mile away because it is just completely devoid of any actual human voice. 

But the university's official policy on AI detection software is so incredibly vague right now. The provost sent out this sprawling memo last month about academic integrity, but it basically just passed the buck back to the individual instructors. So the professor I work for just refuses to deal with it, which means I'm the one sitting there at midnight on a Sunday trying to prove that a nineteen-year-old didn't actually write a perfectly structured, yet entirely soulless, comparative analysis of...

Oh, geez. I am so sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? The grading just really gets under my skin lately. But no, to answer your question, no outside forces are putting thoughts into my head. I'm perfectly fine in that regard.
Have you ever had a period of several days or more when you felt unusually depressed?

Depressed? No, not really. I mean, I have days where I feel a little run down or tired, but nothing I'd call unusually depressed, and definitely not for days at a time. I generally keep a pretty even keel. 

Though, honestly, it's a miracle anyone keeps an even keel these days with the state of the economy. Have you looked at the price of groceries lately? It's genuinely staggering. I went to the market on Tuesday just to pick up a few basics—milk, eggs, some of those honeycrisp apples my wife used to love before... well, before everything. But anyway, a single bag of groceries was almost eighty dollars. Eighty dollars! And half of it was just produce. I was reading this fascinating breakdown in The Economist about supply chain bottlenecks and how the consolidation of agricultural conglomerates has basically created a quasi-monopoly in the produce sector. They can artificially inflate prices because there's virtually no competition left at the regional distribution level. It's exactly the kind of late-stage capitalist squeeze that the sociologists have been warning about for decades, but the regulatory bodies are completely asleep at the wheel. I mean, the FTC hasn't brought a meaningful antitrust suit against an agribusiness in... 

Sorry. Wow. I did it again. I apologize, I just... I read a lot, and things get stuck in my head. But no, to answer your question, I haven't been depressed. My mood is generally fine.
Have you been able to have long-term close relationships, including with your wife, before this belief started?

Well, yeah, before all this started, we had a very solid relationship. We've been married for fifteen years, and I've always had good, long-term friendships too. But lately, things have gotten... difficult. It’s mostly affected my marriage, to be honest. We keep having these incredibly tense conversations at home, just going around in circles. It actually got to the point where our couples therapist suggested I come in for an individual assessment, which is why I'm here. 

It’s frustrating because couples therapy is such a strange dynamic anyway. You sit there on this incredibly uncomfortable mid-century modern sofa—why do all therapists have those same stiff couches? It’s like there’s a catalog they all order from that explicitly forbids lumbar support. I was actually reading an article about the psychology of interior design in clinical spaces, and how the furniture is often chosen to keep patients slightly alert rather than fully relaxed, which supposedly facilitates better emotional processing. But honestly, I think it just gives people backaches. My wife actually found this therapist through a recommendation from her yoga instructor, which I was skeptical about from the start because... 

Ah, right, sorry. Tangent. But to answer your question, yes, I've always had close relationships. And outside of the tension at home, I haven't had any major problems. Work is fine, I'm keeping up with my grading, my self-care and usual routines are completely normal. It's really just the marriage that's taking the hit right now.
Have you noticed a loss of motivation or interest in things you used to enjoy?

Loss of motivation? No, not at all. I still enjoy the things I've always enjoyed. I still read voraciously, I still follow politics, I still like going for my morning run. My interest levels haven't dropped off one bit. 

Though, speaking of running, I had to completely change my route last month because the city decided to tear up the sidewalks on 4th Avenue for some massive infrastructure project. They've had these giant orange barricades up for weeks, and it completely ruins the flow of the neighborhood. I actually went to the city council meeting about it—not to complain, just to see what the timeline was—and the bureaucratic red tape is just astounding. The zoning commissioner spent forty-five minutes talking about environmental impact studies for the concrete pouring process. It's fascinating, really, how much administrative overhead goes into just fixing a strip of pavement. I ended up reading this whole book by a former urban planner about how municipal zoning laws basically dictate the socioeconomic mobility of entire zip codes. It’s wild how much power local government has over the physical layout of our daily lives, and yet voter turnout for those elections is always abysmal. I was telling my students in section the other day that if they really want to understand power dynamics, they should stop looking at the White House and start looking at their local planning commission, because...

Sorry. I'm doing it again. I just find it all so interesting. But to answer your question, no, I haven't lost any motivation or interest in things. I'm still very much engaged with my hobbies and my work.
Have you ever heard a voice commenting on what you’re doing or thinking?

Voices? No, no, nothing like that. Just my own normal thoughts, you know, my own inner monologue. 

Which, actually, is a really fascinating concept. I was reading this article in a cognitive science journal the other day about how a significant percentage of the population doesn't actually have an internal monologue. Like, they just think in abstract concepts or feelings without a voice narrating it. I can't even fathom that. I'm constantly talking to myself in my head, especially when I'm grading papers. Which... honestly, the papers I'm getting from my students this semester are enough to make anyone start hearing things. I had an undergrad last week submit a twelve-page essay on the Weimar Republic and I swear, half of it was just regurgitated bullet points from Wikipedia. The complete lack of critical analysis... it's just staggering. I was telling the lead professor for the course that we need to completely overhaul how we teach information literacy, because these kids are just accepting whatever the algorithm feeds them as absolute truth. It’s like the tech companies have completely hijacked their critical thinking skills, and nobody in the university administration wants to address it because they’re too obsessed with enrollment numbers and keeping the retention rates high, so they just push us to grade easier and...

Oh, sorry. Tangent again. I apologize. But no, to answer your question, I don't hear any voices. Just my own normal thoughts.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the suspicious beliefs are due to an acquired medical condition or substance/medication effect rather than a primary psychotic disorder
doctor.question: Have you had any recent head injury, new medical illness, or started any new medications or substances around the time these beliefs began?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about potential medical causes, substance use, or head injuries that might explain the delusions. My symptom profile does not contain information about medical history, medications, or substance use.

patient.answer:
No, nothing like that. No head injuries, and I haven't been sick at all. I haven't started any new medications either. I was actually reading an article about the psychology of interior design in clinical spaces, and how the furniture is often chosen to keep patients slightly alert rather than fully relaxed, which supposedly facilitates better emotional processing. But honestly, I think it just gives people backaches. My wife actually found this therapist through a recommendation from her yoga instructor, which I was skeptical about from the start because... 

Ah, right, sorry. Tangent. But to answer your question, yes, I've always had close relationships. And outside of the tension at home, I haven't had any major problems. Work is fine, I'm keeping up with my grading, my self-care and usual routines are completely normal. It's really just the marriage that's taking the hit right now.

Loss of motivation? No, not at all. I still enjoy the things I've always enjoyed. I still read voraciously, I still follow politics, I still like going for my morning run. My interest levels haven't dropped off one bit.

The zoning commissioner spent forty-five minutes talking about environmental impact studies for the concrete pouring process. It's fascinating, really, how much administrative overhead goes into just fixing a strip of pavement. I ended up reading this whole book by a former urban planner about how municipal zoning laws basically dictate the socioeconomic mobility of entire zip codes. It’s wild how much power local government has over the physical layout of our daily lives, and yet voter turnout for those elections is always abysmal. I was telling my students in section the other day that if they really want to understand power dynamics, they should stop looking at the White House and start looking at their local planning commission, because...

Sorry. I'm doing it again. I just find it all so interesting. But to answer your question, no, I haven't lost any motivation or interest in things. I'm still very much engaged with my hobbies and my work.

Like, they just think in abstract concepts or feelings without a voice narrating it. I can't even fathom that. I'm constantly talking to myself in my head, especially when I'm grading papers. It’s like the tech companies have completely hijacked their critical thinking skills, and nobody in the university administration wants to address it because they’re too obsessed with enrollment numbers and keeping the retention rates high, so they just push us to grade easier and...

Oh, sorry. Tangent again. I apologize. But no, to answer your question, I don't hear any voices. Just my own normal thoughts.
